hook.situation: You are viewing a studio through a real-estate office and need to ask the questions that change the real cost: deposit, monthly rent, maintenance fee, included utilities, options, and contract details.
objectives: Ask about 보증금, 월세, 관리비, and what is included.
Describe the room and layout with housing nouns and adjective modifiers.
Use 조건, 가능, 목적, and 준비 patterns for real housing decisions.
hook.whyItMatters: Housing Korean is full of words that come as a set. 원룸 without 보증금, 월세, 관리비, 포함되다, and 계약서 is not enough for the real task.

grammarNotes.title: N이/가 있어요 — saying what a home has
grammarNotes.func: Use 있어요 to say a room or feature exists in a home. It is the everyday way to describe what an apartment or house comes with: a balcony, an elevator, parking, and so on.

formTable.ex: 방 → 방이 있어요 (there is a room)
엘리베이터 → 엘리베이터가 있어요 (there is an elevator)

examples.ko: 이 집에 방이 세 개 있어요.
examples.romanization: i jibe bangi se gae isseoyo.
examples.en: This house has three rooms.
examples.note: 방 ends in a consonant, so it takes 이; 있어요 says the rooms exist.

examples.en: Our apartment has an elevator.
examples.note: 엘리베이터 ends in a vowel, so it takes 가.

examples.en: There is a big supermarket near the house.
examples.note: 있어요 also covers 'there is X nearby,' a common housing detail.

examples.en: Is there a balcony?
examples.note: A rising tone turns the statement into a yes/no question renters actually ask.

keyPoint.label: 있어요 vs 이에요/예요
keyPoint.body: 있어요 means 'there is / it has' (existence). 이에요/예요 means 'it is' (identity). 방이 있어요 = 'there is a room'; 방이에요 = 'it is a room.' For listing what a home has, you almost always want 있어요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 있어요 links the 받침 ㅆ into the next vowel: [이써요]. So 방이 있어요 runs together as [방이 이써요].

drill.instruction: Add 이 or 가 to the noun and finish with 있어요 to say the home has it.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English drops the subject marker ('the house has rooms'), but Korean normally needs 이/가 on the thing that exists. Don't omit the particle before 있어요 in careful speech.

grammarNotes.title: N이/가 없어요 — saying a home lacks something
grammarNotes.func: 없어요 is the negative of 있어요: it says a feature does NOT exist. In housing talk it covers a missing room, no parking, no elevator, or 'there is no extra fee.'

formTable.ex: 창문 → 창문이 없어요 (there is no window)
엘리베이터 → 엘리베이터가 없어요 (there is no elevator)

examples.en: This room has no window.
examples.note: 창문 ends in a consonant → 이 없어요; says the feature is absent.

examples.en: This building has no elevator.
examples.note: 엘리베이터 ends in a vowel → 가 없어요.

examples.en: There's no extra cost besides the deposit.
examples.note: A reassuring rental phrase: 없어요 = 'there is no (extra fee).'

examples.en: There are no empty rooms right now.
examples.note: 빈방 'empty room' + 이 없어요 = a common reply from a landlord.

keyPoint.label: 있어요 ↔ 없어요
keyPoint.body: These are a fixed pair, not 있어요 + 안. To say a home lacks something, use 없어요, never 안 있어요. 방이 있어요 (has a room) ↔ 방이 없어요 (has no room).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 없어요 links the cluster ㅄ so only ㅅ carries over: [업써요]. So 창문이 없어요 sounds like [창무니 업써요].

drill.instruction: Use 이/가 없어요 to say the home lacks the feature.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: There is no '안 있어요.' The negative of 있어요 is the separate word 없어요. Reach for 없어요 directly instead of negating 있어요 with 안.

grammarNotes.title: A-(으)ㄴ N — describing a home (넓은 방)
grammarNotes.func: Turn a descriptive adjective into a word that modifies a noun, like 'a spacious room' or 'a clean house.' This is how you describe homes: 넓은 방, 깨끗한 집, 조용한 동네.

formTable.when: Adjective stem ends in a consonant (받침)
Adjective stem ends in a vowel

examples.en: I'm looking for a spacious room.
examples.note: 넓다 (consonant stem) → 넓은 modifies 방; the adjective comes before the noun.

examples.en: I like a clean house.
examples.note: 하다-adjective 깨끗하다 → 깨끗한 (drop the vowel-ending 하, add ㄴ).

examples.en: I want to live in a quiet neighborhood.
examples.note: 조용하다 → 조용한; describes the kind of 동네 (neighborhood).

examples.en: I'm looking for a house close to work.
examples.note: 가깝다 is ㅂ-irregular → 가까운 집; a very common housing criterion.

keyPoint.label: 넓은 방 vs 방이 넓어요
keyPoint.body: Modifier form goes BEFORE the noun: 넓은 방 ('a spacious room' — naming a thing). Predicate form ends the sentence: 방이 넓어요 ('the room is spacious' — stating a fact). Use 넓은 방 when the adjective is labeling the noun.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 넓다 is pronounced [널따], and 넓은 links the ㄼ cluster as [널븐]. 가까운 and 깨끗한 link smoothly.

drill.instruction: Make the adjective modify the noun with -(으)ㄴ.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't put a sentence-ending form in the modifier slot. 넓어요 ends a sentence; to attach it to 방 you must change it to the modifier form 넓은. English uses 'wide' in both spots, but Korean changes the ending.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)면 — stating a housing condition
grammarNotes.func: -(으)면 means 'if / when.' Use it to set a condition about a home: 'if it's too expensive...', 'if I like the place...', 'when I sign the contract...'

examples.ko: 방이 너무 비싸면 다른 집을 볼게요.
examples.romanization: bangi neomu bissamyeon dareun jibeul bolgeyo.
examples.en: If the room is too expensive, I'll look at another place.
examples.note: 비싸다 (vowel stem) → 비싸면; sets the condition before the result clause.

examples.en: It'd be nice if it's close to the subway station.
examples.note: 가깝다 → 가까우면 (ㅂ-irregular); '(으)면 좋아요' = 'it'd be nice if.'

examples.en: When you sign the contract, you pay the deposit.
examples.note: 계약하다 → 계약하면; here -(으)면 means 'when/once' for a routine step.

examples.en: If I like the house, I'll sign the contract.
examples.note: 들다 is ㄹ-final → 마음에 들면 (keep ㄹ, add 면); 마음에 들다 = 'to like.'

keyPoint.label: -(으)면 vs -아/어서
keyPoint.body: -(으)면 is a hypothetical 'if/when' — the result depends on the condition. -아/어서 gives an actual reason that already holds. 비싸면 안 사요 = 'if it's expensive, I won't buy.' 비싸서 안 사요 = 'I'm not buying because it's (actually) expensive.'

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a 받침, 으면 links: 좋으면 sounds like [조으면] (ㅎ weakens between vowels). The ㄹ-stem 들면 is simply [들면].

drill.instruction: Attach -(으)면 to make the housing condition.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: ㄹ-final stems do NOT add 으; they keep ㄹ and add 면 directly: 들다 → 들면. Learners over-apply 으면 to every consonant ending, but ㄹ is special here.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 — what's possible/allowed at home
grammarNotes.func: Express that something is possible or allowed in a home: you can park, you can keep a pet, you can move in next week. The opposite, 'cannot,' is V-(으)ㄹ 수 없어요.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a consonant (받침)
Verb stem ends in a vowel

formTable.ex: 키우다 → 키울 수 없어요 (cannot keep a pet)

examples.en: Can I park here?
examples.note: 주차하다 (vowel stem) → 주차할 수 있어요; a yes/no question about what's allowed.

examples.ko: 이 집에서 강아지를 키울 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: i jibeseo gangajireul kiul su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can keep a dog in this house.
examples.note: 키우다 (vowel stem) → 키울 수 있어요; asking about pets is a common rental question.

examples.en: I can move in next week.
examples.note: 이사하다 → 이사할 수 있어요; states a possible move-in time.

examples.en: You can't keep pets here.
examples.note: The negative uses 없어요: 키울 수 없어요 = 'cannot keep.'

keyPoint.label: 있어요 → 없어요 for 'cannot'
keyPoint.body: To make V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 negative, swap 있어요 for 없어요, not 안: 살 수 있어요 (can live) → 살 수 없어요 (cannot live). The 수 (way/possibility) stays; only the existence verb flips.

drill.instruction: Make 'can do' with V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 수 있어요 is pronounced [수 이써요], and the ㄹ before 수 stays light: 살 수 → [살 쑤] (the ㅅ tenses to ㅆ after the ㄹ).

drill.instruction: Make 'can do' with V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 여기에서 주차 안 할 수 있어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: To say 'cannot park,' don't insert 안 into the can-phrase. The negative of (으)ㄹ 수 있어요 is (으)ㄹ 수 없어요. 안 주차하다 would mean 'choose not to park,' which is different from 'not allowed/able to park.'

grammarNotes.title: N에 살아요 — saying where you live
grammarNotes.func: Use 에 + 살아요 to say where you live: in a city, a neighborhood, an apartment, or on a particular floor. 에 marks the place of residence.

formTable.ex: 아파트에 살아요 (I live in an apartment)

examples.en: I live in Busan.
examples.note: 부산 (place) + 에 살아요; 에 marks where you live.

examples.en: I live in a studio apartment right now.
examples.note: 원룸 'one-room/studio' is a very common type of home in Korea.

examples.en: I live on the 5th floor.
examples.note: 층 'floor' + 에 살아요; 5층 is read 오층.

examples.en: Which neighborhood do you live in?
examples.note: 어느 'which' + 동네 + 에 살아요? — a natural getting-to-know-you question.

keyPoint.label: 에 살아요 vs 에서 + action
keyPoint.body: For living (a state), use 에: 서울에 살아요. For an action that happens at a place, use 에서: 집에서 일해요 ('I work at home'). With 살다 specifically, Korean uses 에, not 에서.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 살아요 links the ㄹ into the next vowel: [사라요]. 부산에 살아요 runs together as [부사네 사라요].

drill.instruction: Add 에 살아요 to say where you live.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: With 살다 (to live/reside), the standard particle is 에, not 에서. English 'live in/at' tempts learners toward 에서, but residence as a state takes 에.

grammarNotes.title: N(으)로 이사 가요/와요 — moving house
grammarNotes.func: Use (으)로 to mark the destination you move TO when changing homes: 이사 가다 'to move (away to)' and 이사 오다 'to move (here to).' (으)로 means 'to / toward.'

formTable.when: Place ends in a vowel or ㄹ

formTable.ex: 새집으로 이사 와요 (move into a new house)

examples.en: I'm moving to a new house next month.
examples.note: 새집 'new house' + 으로 (받침 ㅂ) + 이사 가요; (으)로 marks the destination.

examples.en: I'm going to move to Busan.
examples.note: 부산 ends in ㄴ → 으로; 이사 갈 거예요 = future 'will move.'

examples.ko: 우리 옆집에 새 이웃이 이사 왔어요.
examples.romanization: uri yeopjibe sae iusi isa wasseoyo.
examples.en: A new neighbor moved in next door.
examples.note: 이사 오다 → 이사 왔어요 (past); 옆집 'next-door house,' 이웃 'neighbor.'

examples.en: When are you moving out?
examples.note: 언제 'when' + 이사 가요? — a natural question to a friend who's moving.

keyPoint.label: 이사 가요 vs 이사 와요
keyPoint.body: 이사 가다 = move away (the speaker is not at the destination). 이사 오다 = move here (toward the speaker's location). 서울로 이사 가요 = 'I'm moving to Seoul'; 여기로 이사 왔어요 = 'I moved here.'

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 이사 가요 is [이사 가요]; 으로 links its ㄹ into 이사: 새집으로 → [새지브로]. 이사 왔어요 sounds like [이사 와써요].

drill.instruction: Add (으)로 이사 가요 to say where you're moving to.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: For the destination of a move, Korean prefers (으)로 ('toward/to') with 이사 가다, not 에. English 'move to a new house' suggests 에, but the directional (으)로 is the natural choice here.

exampleSentence.en: How much is the deposit for this studio?
I went to a real-estate office to find a place.
exampleSentence.note: In daily speech, 부동산 often means the office.
Must be asked together with 월세.

exampleSentence.en: I am looking for a monthly-rent studio rather than jeonse.

exampleSentence.note: Small word that changes total cost.

exampleSentence.en: Internet is included in the maintenance fee.

exampleSentence.note: Prepared action before signing or moving.

exampleSentence.en: You can sign the contract today.
exampleSentence.note: Real-estate action after checking the listing.

exampleSentence.en: There is a refrigerator in the kitchen.
I asked the licensed agent about the maintenance fee.
exampleSentence.note: The person helping with the contract.

extendedDialogue.setting: A tenant checks rent, deposit, utilities, and contract preparation at a real-estate office.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: How much is the deposit for this studio?
lines.grammarNote: 원룸 and 보증금 belong together in listing questions.

lines.speaker: 중개사
lines.en: The deposit is 5 million won and the monthly rent is 700,000 won.
lines.grammarNote: 은/는 separates the two money topics clearly.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Is the maintenance fee separate? Is internet included too?
lines.grammarNote: 따로 and 포함되다 are the key fee-boundary words.

lines.speaker: 중개사
lines.en: The maintenance fee is 70,000 won, and internet is included.
lines.grammarNote: 인터넷 is the subject of 포함돼 있어요.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.ko: 이사하기 전에 계약서를 확인해 두면 되죠?
lines.romanization: isahagi jeone gyeyakseoreul hwaginhae dumyeon doejyo?
lines.en: I should check the contract before moving, right?
lines.grammarNote: 확인해 두다 means check it in advance and keep it ready.

lines.speaker: 중개사
lines.ko: 네. 마음에 들면 오늘 계약할 수 있어요.
lines.romanization: ne. maeume deulmyeon oneul gyeyakal su isseoyo.
lines.en: Yes. If you like it, you can sign the contract today.
lines.grammarNote: 면 sets the condition; ㄹ 수 있어요 gives possibility.

readingText.title: 관리비에 인터넷이 포함돼 있어요?
readingText.body: 하나는 이사하기 위해 부동산에 갔어요. 공인중개사는 넓은 원룸 하나를 보여 줬어요. 보증금은 500만 원이고 월세는 70만 원이었어요. 하나는 관리비가 따로인지, 인터넷이 관리비에 포함돼 있는지 물어봤어요. 베란다는 없었지만 부엌에 냉장고와 세탁기가 있었고 화장실도 깨끗했어요. 마음에 들면 오늘 계약할 수 있다고 해서, 하나는 계약하기 전에 계약서를 다시 확인해 두었어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Hana went to a real-estate office to move. The licensed agent showed her a spacious studio. The deposit was 5 million won and the monthly rent was 700,000 won. Hana asked whether the maintenance fee was separate and whether internet was included in the fee. There was no balcony, but there was a refrigerator and washing machine in the kitchen, and the bathroom was clean. Since she could sign the contract that day if she liked it, Hana checked the contract again before signing.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 하나가 확인한 비용 두 가지는 뭐예요?

culturalNote.title: The real cost is not only 월세
culturalNote.body: In Korean rentals, 월세 is only one part of the monthly burden. 보증금 is paid up front, 관리비 may be separate, and utilities such as internet, water, gas, or electricity may or may not be included. A good housing conversation checks all of these before 계약하다.
culturalNote.tip: Ask in this order: 보증금이 얼마예요? 월세가 얼마예요? 관리비는 따로예요? 뭐가 포함돼 있어요? 계약서 먼저 확인해도 돼요?

inlineExercises.prompt: At a real-estate office, which pair belongs together?
inlineExercises.explanation: 보증금 and 월세 are core housing price terms.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which question checks whether a fee is separate?
inlineExercises.explanation: 따로 means separately and is essential for fee questions.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence asks whether internet is included?
inlineExercises.explanation: The included item is the subject, and 관리비 takes 에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Before moving, the prepared-action sentence is:
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 두세요 means do it in advance and leave it prepared.
Vㄹ/을 수 있어요 expresses practical possibility.

inlineExercises.prompt: 관리비___ 포함돼요? (Is the maintenance fee included?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 포함되다 is passive/included, so 관리비 is the subject and takes 가. 를 would fit an active verb like 포함하다.
포함되다 becomes 포함돼요 in polite speech. As a question, rising intonation or the question mark makes it “is it included?”
인터넷이 is the subject of being included. 포함돼요? is the natural real-estate question.
보증금은 sets the deposit as the topic. 얼마예요 asks for the amount or price.
내다 is an active verb, so 월세 is its object and takes 를. 가 would make the rent the subject, which does not fit paying.

bullets: Cost set: 보증금, 월세, 관리비, 따로, 포함되다.
Housing nouns: 원룸, 거실, 부엌, 화장실, 베란다, 현관.
Listing descriptions: 넓은 원룸, 밝은 방, 조용한 동네, 깨끗한 화장실.
Decision patterns: 마음에 들면, 계약할 수 있어요, 집을 구하기 위해, 확인해 두세요.
Contract habit: check 계약서 before 계약하다.

writingTask.prompt: Message a friend about a studio apartment you saw at the real-estate office: describe what it has and lacks, say where it is, and add a condition about whether you'll take it.
writingTask.hint: Use N이/가 있어요/없어요 (거실은 있는데 주차장은 없어요), an adjective + noun (넓은 방), N에 살아요 for location, and -(으)면 for the condition (월세가 싸면 계약할 거예요).
writingTask.model: 오늘 부동산에서 원룸을 봤는데, 넓은 방하고 깨끗한 부엌이 있어요. 그런데 주차장은 없어요. 조용한 동네에 있어서 마음에 들어요. 월세가 너무 비싸지 않으면 다음 달에 이사 가려고 해요.
writingTask.modelEn: I saw a studio at the real-estate office today, and it has a spacious room and a clean kitchen. But there's no parking lot. It's in a quiet neighborhood, so I like it. If the monthly rent isn't too expensive, I'm planning to move in next month.

canDo: Say what a home has or lacks with N이/가 있어요/없어요 (주차장이 없어요)
Describe a home with adjective + noun (넓은 방, 깨끗한 집, 조용한 동네)
State a housing condition with -(으)면 (싸면 계약할 거예요)
Say where I live and where I'm moving with N에 살아요 / N(으)로 이사 가요
